pulls.title: ci: inline runner selection
pulls.body:
We are currently sometimes backlogged on waiting for runner selection.

Selecting Warp or GitHub-hosted runners directly from the repository context avoids serializing all CI jobs behind a metadata job. This keeps forks on public runners while allowing upstream jobs to schedule immediately on the intended runner labels.

This will make the changes needed for "a fork also wanting to use warp runners" slightly larger, but I think that number of people is zero.

pulls.title: [29.x] Finalise 29.5
Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~52 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a five-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: fuzz: check GetStale() returns exactly the stale private broadcast txs
pulls.body:
The `private_broadcast` fuzz test checks each tx that `GetStale()` returns. This adds to it by checking that all stale txs are returned.  `ReattemptPrivateBroadcast()` only retries what `GetStale()` returns, and a stale tx left out is never retried.

This partly came up during review in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35129#pullrequestreview-4427536924, and recently also surfaced in https://mutanthub.space/mutants/3752 , where changing `continue` to `break` in `GetStale()` passes all current tests.

This PR records when each tx is added and when each node confirms it. Then it checks that `GetStale()` returns exactly the expected txs.

pulls.title: Improve loadtxoutset performance
pulls.body:
Significantly improves loadtxoutset performance via a number of changes:

 * parallel threads for decoding, hashing, serializing and writing to leveldb
 * no fsync() gating writes
 * no redundant loading into CoinsView
 
Also adds a subcommand to bitcoin-util for getting a snapshot's hash_serialized_3, muhash, coin count and total amount values without importing to leveldb first.

On my systems, performance ends up bottlenecked by leveldb CPU usage.

pulls.title: net: enforce timeout interval for paused send peers
pulls.body: Today it's possible to keep some peers running ancient versions paused for a long time. If such a peer is so slow to read as to not drain our send buffer down to the 1MB threshold within a reasonable time frame, we really shouldn't be wasting a connection slot on them. I picked 20 minutes as the reasonable time frame, since it's what we already use for ping timeouts today.

pulls.title: refactor: store positions as a 64 bits integer in flatfiles
pulls.body: That field is the last 32-bit in flat files management that is only bounded indirectly by callers' usage (unlike the file number for instance). In the spirit of the ongoing effort to avoid unnecessarily using 32 bits integers or platform specific types (for instance #24214, #33724, #34109, #35097, #35616), i was scanning for fields it could be prudent to promote to prevent any possible future misuse. This one is a good candidate because it does not change on-disk representation, since we serialize positions as varints.

pulls.title: [32.x] Finalise 32.1
mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: allow retrying loadtxoutset after an interrupted load
pulls.body:
**Problem:** An interrupted `loadtxoutset` can leave an incomplete `chainstate_snapshot` database without its required `base_blockhash` marker. A later call can fail to open that database, requiring the operator to remove it manually before retrying.

**Fix:** Wipe the snapshot database before opening it so a later call can replace incomplete data. LevelDB acquires the database lock before deleting files, so a database held open by another load cannot be wiped. Also correct the startup warning to identify the missing marker and explain that retrying replaces the directory.

rpc: Optionally print feerates in sat/vb
pulls.body:
Part of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32093

Returning feerates in BTC/kvB it can be very burdensome and is not good practice, as the most widely adopted units are sat/vB.

The RPC affectd by this PR are `getmempoolinfo`, `getnetworkinfo`, `getwalletinfo`, `estimatesmartfee` and `estimaterawfee`.

Because of sub 1sat/vB environment we cannot rely on GetFee() because it internally uses FeeFrac EvaluateFee() function which rounds the values to always return an int. If the `feerate < 1` then it will be rounded to 1 or 0.

For more context or discuss how to migrate also arguments please refer to the open issue https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32093.

pulls.title: net: reimplement private broadcast as jobs isolated from the node
pulls.body:
Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to
the connection manager. Each job runs on its own thread, shares no state with the node, and
reaches the network only through the Tor proxy: it resolves the chain's DNS seeds, then announces
over BIP324 to recipients on a schedule drawn up front, each connection with fresh isolation
credentials. Nothing a recipient does, and nothing the node sees of the transaction coming back,
changes the plan, and the transaction enters the node's mempool only when it returns from the
network. The old private broadcast connections and relay are removed.

The invariants are specified in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`.

The rest of the tests are in a follow-up to be considered later:
https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup

pulls.title: validation: check the most recent AssumeUTXO commitment during IBD
pulls.body:
**Problem:** AssumeUTXO verifies imported UTXOs against a hash we bake into the binary.
Every node reconstructs the same UTXO set during ordinary IBD, but [does not check its hash against the existing AssumeUTXO commitment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32377).

**Fix:** During ordinary block validation, verify the provided AssumeUTXO hash when block connection reaches the corresponding block, stopping the node on a mismatch.
Flush pending changes to disk before hashing the UTXO set and comparing the result with the commitment.

Keep only the latest AssumeUTXO commitment per network to limit the extra hashing work during IBD, and update the release process to replace it.
Users who need older snapshots for research or other purposes can use a compatible older release or restore the corresponding commitment as `m_assumeutxo_data` and recompile.

pulls.title: script: prevent partial reinitialization of sighash data
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `PrecomputedTransactionData` could be default-constructed and filled later with `Init()`.
That allowed an object to exist without transaction-specific data and left a public reuse path that was easy to get wrong.
The old `Init()` guard only checked [`m_spent_outputs_ready`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/2063f02bd5edebe1b5c9635db8850220811ebc90/src/script/interpreter.cpp#L1415), which remained false after initialization without spent outputs even when the BIP143 prevout, sequence, and output hashes were already cached.
No current caller reuses an object across transactions, so validation and signing results are unchanged.
`btck_script_pubkey_verify()` in the experimental kernel C API also copied caller-supplied txdata on each verification call.

**Fix:** Remove default construction and `Init()` so each `PrecomputedTransactionData` object is built for one transaction.
Callers that already have the transaction and optional spent outputs construct it directly.
Validation stores txdata in `std::optional` and emplaces it only after a script-cache miss, keeping precomputation lazy.
`ConnectBlock()` also leaves txdata storage empty when assumevalid skips script checks, covering #35663.
The kernel verification path binds directly to caller-supplied txdata and constructs a local fallback only when needed.

pulls.title: sock: align exception monitoring between poll() and select() backends
pulls.body:
On non-Linux platforms, `WaitMany` monitors every socket for exceptional conditions, even when we are not looking to read from it. On Linux, it never monitors those.

Monitoring for certain socket events on some platforms but not others is inconsistent and surprising. In this instance it probably means these cases receive less testing as well, since they are ignored on our most well-tested platform.

Fix this issue by only monitoring for exceptional conditions (which is necessary to detect failed connection attempts early on Windows) for sockets we are also waiting to read from.

pulls.title: torcontrol: send -torpassword hex-encoded to avoid escaping bugs
pulls.body:
The Tor password was sent as a `QuotedString` with only double quotes escaped; as Tor interprets backslash escapes inside it, any password containing a backslash was mangled (or left the string unterminated).

The Tor Control spec deliberately allows the token to be sent as unquoted hex "to avoid escaping issues", as the `SAFECOOKIE` response already is. This patch does the same for the password, and also adds a functional test covering backslashes and quotes.

pulls.title: net: don't discourage private broadcast peers
pulls.body:
Discouraging a private broadcast connection may be observable.

pulls.title: private broadcast: wait synchronously for mempool acceptance
pulls.body:
Calling `BroadcastTransaction` with the `NO_MEMPOOL_PRIVATE_BROADCAST` method skips inserting the transaction into the mempool and returns immediately. This causes problems with software that expects the transaction to be in the mempool after the function returns. For example many third-party wallets or services call `sendrawtransaction` and expect the transaction to be in the mempool after it returns a successful response.

This PR adds a new `TransactionAddedToMempoolSync` method to `CValidationInterface`. This is then used in `BroadcastTransaction` when the method is `NO_MEMPOOL_PRIVATE_BROADCAST` to wait for the transaction to have been accepted back into the mempool before returning. It also adds a timeout (default 10 minutes) to `BroadcastTransaction` and exposes it as an option for `sendrawtransaction`. Setting the timeout to 0 disables the wait and returns immediately, preserving the current behavior.

Synchronously waiting for mempool acceptance is also a prerequisite for adding private broadcast support to the wallet. The `TransactionAddedToMempoolSync` method is added specifically for future wallet broadcasting, so a broadcast caller holding `cs_wallet` will not timeout waiting on another background event that is also trying to acquire `cs_wallet`.

pulls.title: addrman: apply time penalty in nTime check
pulls.body:
There is an existing check in `AddSingle()` that prevents us from increasing the `RefCount` of an address when the same announcement is received again from a different peer, which regularly happens with gossip relay - an addr can take different routes through the network to us.

However, the check is ineffective: when the entry was first added, its `nTime` was stored with a [2h time penalty](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/9d4325f40316d2c81d34418dc075b235173d0cec/src/net_processing.cpp#L6044) applied, so `addr.nTime > pinfo->nTime` holds even for an identical announcement. As a result, a single announcement relayed to us by several peers could increase an address's multiplicity in the new table, up to 8.

Fix this by applying the penalty in the comparison too, matching the `nTime` update check a few lines above.

This is just a small logic bugfix, it doesn't change things in adversarial scenarios, since peers can just do multiple announcements with changed `nTime` if they want to boost their `RefCount` artificially.

pulls.title: net: Use exclusive P2P listen sockets on Windows
pulls.body:
on Windows, `SO_REUSEADDR` does not carry over the same semantics as on
POSIX systems. a second socket can set `SO_REUSEADDR` and bind to a
port that is _already in use_ by another process running under
the _same_ user account. this means another local process could bind to
the P2P listen port and receive incoming connections intended for
`bitcoind`.

this matters because the P2P listener is expected to have exclusive
ownership of its address and port. allowing another process to bind to
it could let that process _intercept_ incoming P2P connections. this is
in a similar spirit to #36169, which made the RPC listener exclusive on
Windows.

to fix this, we use `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` for the P2P listen socket on
Windows instead of `SO_REUSEADDR`, while retaining `SO_REUSEADDR` on
other platforms. the added test verifies the expected behaviour by
attempting to bind a second socket to the same port. on Windows, this
fails with `WSAEACCES` (`10013`), which Python exposes as
`PermissionError` (an `OSError` subclass).

references:

- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winsock/using-so-reuseaddr-and-so-exclusiveaddruse
- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14388706/how-do-so-reuseaddr-and-so-reuseport-differ/14388707#14388707

`EventLoop::loop()` exits when its reference count reaches zero. In `serve()` mode, the parent connection is the only reference keeping the loop running. Other `CapnpProtocol` methods called from threads not handling parent IPC requests do not hold their own references and therefore depend on the parent connection remaining alive.

Add `loopRef()` (code suggested by @ryanofsky in https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/376#discussion_r4268952676), which returns a new reference to the event loop or throws if the loop is not running or is shutting down, and use it in the methods that need the loop. Protect `m_loop` with a new `m_loop_mutex` to prevent `serve()` from destroying the loop while `loopRef()` is accessing it.

pulls.title: kernel, validation: Add btck_chainstate_manager_set_clock_time
pulls.body:
The main commit in this PR is the second commit adding a `btck_chainstate_manager_set_clock_time` API which lets kernel applications run validation code deterministically without depending on the system clock. This is an alternative to #35496, and one of several alternatives discussed in that PR, with some tradeoffs described in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35496#issuecomment-4735710317. The other commits are indirectly related and could be moved to separate PRs (or dropped):
Details

- The first commit fixes a timing race in the `chainstatemanager_ibd_exit_after_loading_blocks` test that happened because test code and validation code (in `UpdateIBDStatus`) were both calling `NodeClock::now()` to get the current clock time, and test relied on the times being the same for `tip_recent=true` checks. The failure this fixes should be rare, but I noticed it when I experimented with making time comparison in `IsTipRecent` more precise. - The third commit refactors mempool code to use a consistent way of getting and representing clock times, allowing the fourth commit to enforce that no libbitcoinkernel code uses nondeterministic clock times unintentionally. The third and fourth commits do not need to be part of this PR, but I implemented them to be sure the main commit was complete and all call sites were using the right clock times.

pulls.title: init: refuse -bytespersigop values that overflow
pulls.body:
`-bytespersigop` is parsed as int64, stored as unsigned int, and multiplied by a transaction's sigop cost into the int32 sizes used by the mempool. Negative values wrap, values of 2^32 or more are truncated (4294967296 turns the sigop adjustment off), and large values overflow, so a debug build aborts on an `Assume`. The first commit refuses any value outside [0, 21474] at startup: up to 21474, a package of 25 transactions at the standard sigops limit still has an int32 size.

The second commit checks the sigops limit before a transaction is staged. A transaction that is otherwise standard can be far over that limit, and at 21474 one with about 100,000 sigops still overflows when staged. `mempool_sigoplimit.py` covers the range, a 25-transaction package at 21474, and that transaction.

pulls.title: rpc: add cpu_load to getpeerinfo
pulls.body:
Add a new field `cpu_load` to the output of `getpeerinfo` RPC.

It represents the CPU time spent by the message handling thread for the given peer, weighted for the duration of the connection. That is, for example, if two peers are equally demanding and one is connected longer than the other, then they will have the same `cpu_load` number.

---

Monitoring CPU usage is useful on its own. Also related to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/31033.

---

This PR uses `clock_gettime()` (POSIX) and `GetThreadTimes()` (Windows). An alternative to those, should this be explored are: `getrusage()` (POSIX) and `QueryThreadCycleTime()` (Windows, but it counts CPU cycles).

pulls.body:
We currently concentrate the validation of all the assigned peer’s reconsiderable orphans that are still missing inputs in a single message-processing turn. This ties orphan processing to validation result, and adds latency to processing other peers' messages.

Always process a single reconsiderable orphan per turn instead. This removes the need for an immediate validation result, and shifts the latency from other peers to the assigned peer.

pulls.title: kernel: Add function for setting prune target in ChainstateManagerOptions
pulls.body:
### Motivation & Background

Currently, the libbitcoinkernel C API does not provide a way to configure block pruning on  tck_ChainstateManagerOptions. Even though the underlying 
ode::BlockManager::Options and 
ode::ChainstateLoadOptions structures support pruning, libbitcoinkernel callers cannot pass a prune target.

Consequently, trying to open an existing pruned node's data directory fails during 
ode::LoadChainstate() with:
``
[error] Failed to load chain state from your data directory: You need to rebuild the database using -reindex to go back to unpruned mode.
``
because chainman.m_blockman.m_have_pruned is true while options.prune defaults to false.

### Description of Changes

1. **C API (src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.h)**:
   - Added  tck_chainstate_manager_options_set_prune_target(opts, prune_target_bytes).
   - Exposed  tck_PRUNE_TARGET_MANUAL (matching 
ode::BlockManager::PRUNE_TARGET_MANUAL) for manual pruning (-prune=1).
   - Exposed  tck_MIN_PRUNE_TARGET_BYTES (550 MiB, matching MIN_DISK_SPACE_FOR_BLOCK_FILES).

2. **Kernel Implementation (src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.cpp)**:
   - Implemented  tck_chainstate_manager_options_set_prune_target().
   - Validates that prune_target_bytes is either 0 (unpruned),  tck_PRUNE_TARGET_MANUAL, or >= btck_MIN_PRUNE_TARGET_BYTES.
   - Sets m_blockman_options.prune_target = prune_target_bytes and m_chainstate_load_options.prune = (prune_target_bytes > 0) under LOCK(opts.m_mutex).

3. **C++ Wrapper & Tests**:
   - Added SetPruneTarget() in src/kernel/bitcoinkernel_wrapper.h.
   - Added boundary tests in src/test/kernel/test_kernel.cpp (verifying rejection of < 550_MiB, acceptance of minimum, manual, and unpruned values).

Fixes #35627.

pulls.title: compressor: oversized script decoding can leave a spendable script
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

**Fix:** Replace the destination with `OP_RETURN` rather than appending it.

Found while reviewing #36280. This predates that PR and appears latent because oversized outputs are excluded from the UTXO set, but it could affect malformed stored records decoded into a reused destination.

pulls.title: validation: bound snapshot cache growth by bytes, not coin count
pulls.body:
Loading a snapshot checks the coins cache against -dbcache only every 120000 coins. A coin can carry a script of up to 10000 bytes. A snapshot file made of such coins can push the cache about 1.2 GB past -dbcache between two checks.

I added a check once the cache has grown by 4 MiB since the last one, and kept the 120000-coin check. Typical coins reach the 4 MiB bound about every 30000 coins. The added cost is negligible. Between checks the cache can still exceed -dbcache by about 4 MiB. I added a case to feature_assumeutxo.py that loads 2000 coins with 10000-byte scripts under -dbcache=4. It fails without the change and passes with it. The coins and validation unit tests pass.

pulls.title: tracing: run USDT tests without BPF privileges
pulls.body:
The USDT functional tests currently use BCC to attach eBPF programs to Bitcoin Core’s tracepoints. This requires BCC, matching kernel headers, and elevated BPF permissions, making the tests awkward to run locally and
requiring a privileged container in CI.

Replace the BCC consumers with GDB. Each tested node runs as a debugger child, allowing the tests to enable the real USDT probes and inspect their arguments when execution reaches the probe location. This continues to test
the parts of the USDT interface provided by Bitcoin Core:

- the probe metadata is present and understood;
- the probes can be enabled and are reached in the expected scenarios; and
- their arguments have the expected values, sizes, and lifetimes.

All five tests can run with GDB and `binutils`, without BCC or matching kernel headers. The ASan CI job no longer needs a privileged container and uses `SYS_PTRACE` instead. This also removes the embedded BPF programs from
the tests, reducing their size and maintenance burden. Overall, the change removes roughly 660 lines of test and CI code.

#### Tradeoffs

- These tests no longer exercise the consumer-side eBPF path, including BCC   compilation, kernel BPF verification and loading, uprobe attachment, BPF-side argument decoding, and perf-buffer delivery. Problems confined to
  those components would no longer be detected here.
- LeakSanitizer is disabled for nodes run under GDB because it cannot operate under `ptrace`. Other sanitizer checks remain enabled.

The remaining coverage is focused on Bitcoin Core’s side of the USDT interface. Testing the general BCC, eBPF, and kernel uprobe is left to those consumers and the kernel.

pulls.title: depends: harden Linux and Windows packages
pulls.body:
The depends packages are built without `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` and `-fstack-clash-protection` unless the compiler turns them on by default. `CMakeLists.txt` adds both to `core_interface` only. The release flags in `depends/hosts/linux.mk` and `mingw32.mk` are only `-O2`. I did not add `-fcf-protection` (see #30685).

In a `debian:trixie` container (GCC 14.2, aarch64) I built depends with `NO_QT=1` and then Core, on master and on this branch. On master no library in depends calls a `_chk` function. pulls.title: test: make p2p_eviction actually exercise block-time protection
pulls.body:
`p2p_eviction.py` tests that 4 inbound peers that recently sent us a novel block are protected from eviction. However, the test currently passes even when that protection is not in effect. 

The block-sending peers are connected first, so they are the oldest connections. Then the youngest remaining peer gets evicted. The check `evicted_peers[0] not in protected_peers` therefore holds whether or not block-time protection works.

A block is therefore stored even if it has less work than the tip, is more than 288 blocks ahead of it, is below the minimum chain work, or was pruned before. Blocks differ because `force_processing` changes what is stored.

A nested `btck_chainstate_manager_import_blocks` call on the same chainstate manager also aborts. I checked both aborts with a small program against the library. pulls.title: http: do not process requests after a closing reply
pulls.body:
The HTTP server runs requests that are already in its receive buffer after it has queued a reply that closes the connection. RFC 9112 section 9.6 says it must not. This is a regression from #35182, which replaced libevent: libevent's `evhttp_send_done()` frees the connection once a closing reply is sent, so buffered requests were never parsed. The server also keeps the connection open after a request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding. Section 6.1 says it must close it. Until both are fixed, a request sent right behind a request with both headers is run.

The first commit stops reading requests from a client once a closing reply is queued or the client is flagged for disconnection. Its code and unit tests are azuchi's work from #36355, which was closed. The second commit makes `WriteReply()` send "Connection: close" for a request with both headers, so the server closes the connection. It extends the Content-Length plus Transfer-Encoding case in `interface_http.py`: a `setnetworkactive false` request sent right behind it must not run, and the only reply must say "Connection: close". Tested with `test_bitcoin --run_test=httpserver_tests` and the functional tests `interface_http.py`, `interface_rpc.py` and `interface_rest.py`, which pass.

pulls.title: coins: warn of low disk space before chainstate compaction
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Full chainstate compaction can temporarily require nearly another copy of the database before old files are deleted.

**Fix:** Log automatic full compaction start and finish at info level. Before starting, check the free space on the chainstate filesystem, and if it is below `m_assumed_chain_state_size`, log a warning and skip this compaction. pulls.title: wallet: fix migration of watch-only wallets with transactions
pulls.body:
Migrating a legacy wallet that holds no spendable material fails whenever the
wallet contains transactions. `migratewallet` returns
`std::bad_function_call (-1)` and the wallet is left unmigrated.

Two defects are involved, and the first one hides the second.

### 1. The migration check reads in-memory state that has not been updated yet

When the wallet being migrated has no spendable material,
`CWallet::ApplyMigrationData()` asserts that nothing is left behind in it:

```cpp
if (!m_address_book.empty()) return util::Error{_("Error: Not all address book records were migrated")};
if (!mapWallet.empty()) return util::Error{_("Error: Not all transaction records were migrated")};
```

The two checks look symmetric but are not. `DelAddressBookWithDB()` erases from
`m_address_book` straight away, so the first check sees current state.
`RemoveTxs()` only erases the transaction records from disk; it defers the
`mapWallet` removal to the db txn's `on_commit` listener, which does not run
until the txn is committed — after `ApplyMigrationData()` has returned.

`mapWallet` is therefore never empty at that point and the check always fails.

### 2. Aborting the txn calls a callback that was never set

`DbTxnListener` declares `on_commit` and `on_abort` as plain `std::function`
members and callers may set only the one they need. `RemoveTxs()` does exactly
that: `on_commit` is set, `on_abort` is left empty.

`TxnCommit()` and `TxnAbort()` each invoked their listener's callback
unconditionally, so the abort triggered by the failed check above threw
`std::bad_function_call`. The exception escaped the wallet entirely, replacing
the real error with an unhelpful one and skipping the caller's cleanup path.

### Fix

The first commit skips callbacks that are not set, and documents that they are
optional. The second discounts the transactions already queued for deletion
instead of requiring `mapWallet` to be empty.

They are kept separate because the second defect masks the first: with only the
listener fix applied, the migration surfaces the real error
`Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)` instead of
`std::bad_function_call (-1)`.

### Testing

`src/wallet/test/db_tests.cpp` gains a regression test covering a listener with
only one callback set, for both commit and abort. It fails on master with
`std::bad_function_call` and passes with the fix.

`test/functional/wallet_migration.py` gains a case migrating a blank legacy
wallet with a watch-only address that has received a transaction. The test is
taken from #36483.

To reproduce on master, apply the functional test alone and run
`wallet_migration.py`.

Fixes #36483

pulls.title: fuzz: add a custom mutator for PSBT
pulls.body:
The `partially_signed_transaction_deserialize` target feeds raw bytes to the PSBT parser. Byte-level mutations rarely produce well-formed key-value maps with valid keydata (pubkeys, xpubs, control blocks, DER signatures, etc), so most inputs are rejected early and the deeper per-field parsing is rarely reached.

This PR adds a custom mutator for PSBT which is ported from bitcoinfuzz (with some changes).  The mutator splits the input into global/input/output maps of key-value records, applies the mutations and serializes the result again. The first commit is a preparation to allow targets to provide a custom mutator by adding an optional `mutator` field to
`FuzzTargetOptions`. 

note: LLM assisted on porting the custom mutator.

pulls.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

pulls.title: private broadcast: Extra guard against unintended non-private broadcast of private transactions
pulls.body:
Motivation: Reduce the risk of accidental privacy leak happening when broadcasting non-privately a requested transaction that had been previously broadcast privately.

Background: During the initial phase of private broadcast implementation there were unforeseen instances when a private transaction could get broadcast non-privately (e.g. see #36277 #36330 #36309).

Currently known pathways:

- Re-submission through `submitpackage`
- Wallet-rebroadcast (when a private transaction is "picked up" by the wallet, and rebrodcast after 1-2 days)

Note that these are being addressed, but other, currently non-identified pathways cannot be excluded.

Change summary: Add a general, extra safeguard: whenever there is a transaction broadcast request, check if the given transaction has been previously broadcast privately, and if so, refuse to broadcast non-privately.

Transaction relay is not affected, as it should not be affected by private broadcast.  When we receive a previously private-broadcast transaction for the first time (it's not yet in our mempool), we relay it as any other relayed transaction. Behavior is unchanged in this regard.

Notes:

- Prerequisite: This is built on top of #36477, as keeping finished private broadcasts in the queue is a prerequisite for this change to work.
- This proposed change is not an alternative to the use-case specific safeguards, but a complementary one.
- Testing currently uses the two pathways listed above. When they are closed, testing will be more difficult (i.e., it is hard to establish whether non-private broadcast is prevented by the use-case specific or the present generic guard).
- The private broadcast queue is not persisted, it doesn't survive node restarts
- Entries deleted via `abortprivatebroadcast` will be forgotten.

pulls.title: Reimplement private broadcast as node state-less jobs + package relay support
pulls.body:
## Goals

Goal 1: Remove reliance on, and probes about, internal node state from private broadcast

Goal 2: Specify observable behavior to aid reimplementation and reduce profile fingerprints across versions

### Layout

Four parts, each starting with an empty marker commit:

1. support: moves shared code into the common library; no behavior change
2. bitcoin-privbcast: the specification and the standalone tool
3. bitcoind -privatebroadcast as jobs: the node runs the tool's job; the old relay and connections are removed
4. package mode: one parent and its child. Its validation commits (saturating fee sum, test-accept as submission, self-paying parent) serve only this part.

For the v33 release, I think 1 through 3 should be the goal, but the roadmap could be trimmed down to remove tool-only code if the conceptual support for the standalone tool is not there.

The tool itself introduces about 600 loc of logic, and also necessitates some of the prep move-only commits putting things in common. The vast majority is the shared Job machinery.


## Node-less state

The primary failure mode of the in-master private broadcast is that it relies on node state for operation, and this has led to a number of "careful coding" fixes:

1. The v2->v1 retry connected directly, without the proxy: #35319 (merged in #35410)
2. Discouraging a misbehaving peer gave a clearnet oracle: #36312
3. Eager job completion via mempool inspection: #36277
4. Private broadcast connections wrote to addrman: #35032

There are many other sources of fingerprints as well, some harder than others to exploit, and to fix. The solution: remove reliance on node state entirely to drive attempts. The spec states the goals as:

- A job reveals neither the sender's IP address, onion address nor node identity to any party.
- A hostile recipient, DNS seed or Tor exit learns no more than an honest one. It can only affect delivery.

### Jobs, slots and opportunities

- **Job**: one broadcast of one transaction, from submission to its report. A job spends its first 12 s finding candidates (IPv4/IPv6 addresses from the DNS seeds, resolved through Tor exits), then delivers. It runs for at most 10 min.
- **Slot**: one of a job's 6 independent delivery targets. Each slot tries to announce the transaction to one peer and serve it when asked. Slots 0–2 open when delivery starts; slot 3 opens 35–180 s later; slots 4–5 open 185–240 s later, at least 5 s apart. Each of these times is drawn at random within its range.
- **Opportunity**: one of a slot's 4 scheduled connection times: a first attempt and up to 3 fallbacks, each 50–60 s after the previous. A fallback runs only if the slot's previous attempt failed before announcing; once a slot announces, its remaining opportunities are dropped.

The times are drawn at job start, and each opportunity's candidate is fixed when discovery ends, before any peer is contacted. Nothing a peer does moves them (C1–C4). A job makes at most 24 connections, at most 6 of them at once.

### Differences at a glance

| | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | Inside `bitcoind` only | `bitcoind -privatebroadcast`, or the standalone `bitcoin-privbcast` with no node; the same job either way (U3), with a JSON report of every connection |
| Recipients | `addrman.Select()` over onion, I2P, and IPv4/IPv6 through the proxy; networks follow `-onlynet` | DNS seed names resolved through Tor exits (RESOLVE), IPv4/IPv6 only; no node state used (R1, R6) |
| Connections | `CConnman` peers of type `PRIVATE_BROADCAST`, visible in `getpeerinfo` | The job's own proxy streams, each with fresh SOCKS credentials, so each gets its own circuit; not peers of the node |
| Plan | 3 connections, then more whenever the tx is stale (5 min, then 1 min) until it comes back from the network | 6 slots of 4 opportunities, all scheduled at job start; no retries; at most 10 min |
| Transport | v2 when addrman advertises it, otherwise v1, with a v2→v1 retry | BIP324 v2 only, with one constant VERSION per release (B4, E1) |
| Node settings | Shape which networks and peers are used | Peer-selection settings don't apply to jobs (U2) |
| Packages | — | `submitpackage` with one parent and one child: announce the child, serve the parent on request |

### No addrman

Under master, the node's private broadcast destinations are drawn from the node's addrman. Other parties write to that table through addr gossip, which makes it a unique fingerprint vector, and inherently attacker influenced. This rules out drawing recipients from anything the node or its peers can write to.

Its replacement is querying DNS seeds in a predetermined way under a static profile. This is inherently less robust than the p2p network in terms of liveness, but leaves no fingerprint within a release. The marginal fingerprint is the set of DNS seeds per release, which affects who is queried and exactly how. Each RESOLVE returns one address and exits cache answers, so each seed is asked through several exits: 4 Tor circuits, each querying all 7 seeds, for up to 28 results, which are assigned to the 6x4 opportunities before any dialing happens. A circuit per query, 28 in all, kept Tor busy enough that overlapping discoveries lost answers.

If the list shrinks, grows, or is modified, the release is revealed to the Tor exits carrying the queries, which see every seed name queried. A DNS seed learns only that it is on the list, and only when the exit has no cached answer.

The fingerprint potential also precludes fixed seeds, which change greatly each release, and which degrade in connectivity over time regardless.

### Minimal release fingerprint

Once a release is cut, behavior profiles are intended to be identical per user. This precludes user knobs and per-instance parameters, and requires a constant user agent and VERSION.

Across releases, the reimplemented p2p message state machine allows better control of unnecessary profile breaks going forward.

### Specification

`doc/design/private-broadcast-tool.md` comes before any code in part 2. It has goals, a threat model per party (recipient, exit, seed, network observer, guard), 54 numbered invariants (A–U, N), parameters, interface, assumptions, non-goals and a rationale. Code comments and tests cite the invariant IDs, so review can check code against a stated property. Concept review of the goals, threat model and non-goals is most useful first, then review of the implementation against the invariants.

This implementation is actually the second implementation, initially implemented solely via the spec and black box tests, which were handed to an otherwise blind agent.

### Tradeoffs

- Needs Tor, including Tor's RESOLVE extension. I2P is gone, and so are onion recipients. To re-add these, we need a connect->GETADDR step, and then have to filter out most of the addresses that do not answer when dialed.
- DNS seeds and Tor exits learn that a job ran, in addition to end recipients.
- No retries beyond the scheduled fallbacks. Retrying would act on whether the transaction comes back, which the adversary controls; the user resubmits instead.
- `getprivatebroadcastinfo` now reports jobs, and the connections no longer show in `getpeerinfo`.

pulls.title: rpc: reset id and version per batch element
pulls.body:
In a JSON-RPC batch, an element that is not an object gets an error reply with the id and version of the element before it.

`ExecuteHTTPRPC` uses one request object for the whole batch. `parse()` throws on a non-object before it resets `id` and `m_json_version`. For `[{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getblockcount","id":"X"}, 2]` the reply has two objects with `"id":"X"`, one with a result and one with an error. If the first element is a notification, the error is dropped. I reset both fields at the top of `parse()`, so the error is the one the first element of a batch already gets. The new case in `interface_rpc.py` fails on master and passes with this change.

This is one of several PRs from a large audit of Bitcoin Core that I did with the help of LLM tools. The audit produced its evidence all at once, which is why the PRs arrive together. I understand each change fully and will answer review questions myself.

pulls.title: node: batch block file pruning in a single pass over block index
pulls.body:
When starting a node with pruning enabled (e.g. `-prune=550`) on a node with full chain history or pruning many files at once, `FindFilesToPrune` and `FindFilesToPruneManual` previously called `PruneOneBlockFile` once per file.

Because `PruneOneBlockFile` iterated over the entire `m_block_index` for each file, this was an O(M * N) operation (M = files to prune, N = total blocks). When pruning a full chain (~5,770 files and ~972k blocks), this triggered ~5.6 billion iterations and froze the node running on a Pi 5 for ~10 minutes on startup while holding `cs_main`.

This PR replaces `PruneOneBlockFile` with `PruneBlockFiles(const std::set<int>&)`, which collects all candidate files and prunes them in a single O(M + N) pass over `m_block_index` using a compact dynamic `bitfield (std::vector<bool>)`. Also skips entries without block or undo data to avoid unneeded checks and prevent file 0 pruning from dirtying header-only or already-pruned index entries. The new signature is analogous to `UnlinkPrunedFiles({file_number});`.

Benchmarked with ~972k blocks and 5,770 files to prune:
- x86_64 (i7-8665U @ 1.90 GHz): 75.1s -> 14.7ms (~5,100x speedup)
- ARM64 (Raspberry Pi 5): 606.0s -> 26.3ms (>3,500x speedup)

Add unit test `blockmanager_prune_block_files_batch` to verify batch pruning, empty set no-ops, and clean dirty-set behavior. Update caller tests in `blockmanager_tests` and `rescan_tests`.

torcontrol: Limit what a Tor control port reply can do
pulls.body:
A program that answers on the Tor control port can hang the node at shutdown and point its onion connections at another host.

I now accept the cookie file named in the PROTOCOLINFO reply only if it is a regular file. A FIFO made `fopen()` block the torcontrol thread, and shutdown waits for that thread. On POSIX the file is opened with `O_NONBLOCK`, so a swap to a FIFO after the check does not block either.

I also use the SOCKS listener from `GETINFO net/listeners/socks` only if it is on the control port's host. That is a loopback address if the control port is on loopback, and the `-torcontrol` host otherwise. Other listeners, including unix sockets, are ignored and a warning is logged. The program can no longer name another host.

If no listener qualifies, I keep the onion proxy set by `-proxy` instead of replacing it with `127.0.0.1:9050`. A remote Tor whose SOCKS listener is on the `-torcontrol` host keeps working. A remote Tor that listens for SOCKS on another address now needs `-onion`, or a `-proxy` that points to it.

Two cases stay open. A program on a loopback control port can still name a loopback listener of its own, and a regular file on a filesystem whose read never returns can still block shutdown.

Tests:
- a unit test for the listener rule in `torcontrol_tests`;
- a FIFO case in `util_tests`;
- functional tests in `feature_torcontrol.py`, with the mock Tor server, for the cookie file and the listeners.

`doc/tor.md` says that the control port is trusted, and a release note describes the change.

pulls.title: doc: describe REST browser risk as DNS rebinding
pulls.body:
The Risks section of `doc/REST-interface.md` describes the wrong way for a web page to read the REST interface.

It says a page can read the node with `<script src="http://127.0.0.1:8332/rest/tx/....json">`. A JSON object is not a valid script, so that reads nothing. The server accepts any `Host` header. A page whose domain name is later made to resolve to `127.0.0.1` (DNS rebinding) can therefore read the interface with same-origin requests. I changed the text to say that. A `Host` check would also stop this, but it needs a list of allowed names, so I left it out. I checked that a REST request with `Host: evil.example` gets a 200. I did not run a rebinding page.

pulls.title: http: update m_keep_alive under m_send_mutex
pulls.body:
`HTTPRemoteClient::Send()` sets `m_keep_alive` before taking `m_send_mutex` and appending the response to the send buffer, while the I/O thread reads it under `m_send_mutex` in `MaybeSendBytesFromBuffer()` right after the buffer drains to empty. The two updates are therefore not ordered with respect to each other, and a pipelining client can lose a response:

1. Response 1 (keep-alive) is partially sent and the I/O thread is still draining it.
2. Request 2 (`Connection: close`) is parsed from the receive buffer and dispatched to a worker (the send throttle from #36174 only holds a request back once the buffer exceeds `MAX_BODY_SIZE`).
3. The worker clears `m_keep_alive`; the I/O thread then finishes sending response 1, sees an empty buffer with `m_keep_alive == false`, and sets `m_disconnect`.
4. The worker appends response 2, which is dropped when the client is disconnected on the next loop iteration.

This PR moves the assignment into the critical section that appends the response, and turns the field from `std::atomic_bool` into a plain `bool GUARDED_BY(m_send_mutex)` so Clang's thread-safety analysis enforces the ordering (the only reader already holds the mutex). With the flag and the buffer updated together, the I/O thread can no longer observe "empty && !keep_alive" between two pipelined responses.

The ordering dates back to the initial HTTP server implementation (#35182); #35829/#36007 only moved the code. The window is small and `bitcoin-cli` does not pipeline, so this is a low-severity fix.

### Test

`http_pipelined_keepalive_close_tests` reproduces the interleaving deterministically with a mock socket: `Send()` fails with EAGAIN until the second request has been dispatched, then the I/O thread's next `Send()` (made while holding `m_send_mutex`) signals the worker to write its reply, waits for it to reach `HTTPRemoteClient::Send()`, and only then flushes the first reply. Sends are refused again until the test releases them, so the second reply is only delivered if the I/O loop kept the connection open. Without the first commit the test fails with `server.GetConnectionsCount() == 1 has failed [0 != 1]`: the client was disconnected with the second reply still in its send buffer.

pulls.title: fuzz: Add a target that feeds arbitrary bytes to V2Transport
pulls.body:
No fuzz target feeds V2Transport bytes that an honest peer would not send past the v2 key exchange. I add p2p_transport_v2_receive. It knows the keys of the transport it tests. It builds the input from arbitrary bytes and from the parts of a valid handshake: the peer key, garbage, the garbage terminator and encrypted packets, which may be corrupted. It feeds the input in pieces of arbitrary size. It reaches every v2 receive state and the failures on the way to them.

I ran it for about 13 minutes in total from an empty corpus, with libFuzzer and the address and undefined sanitizers, and it found no crash. Replaying the corpus gets both accepted and rejected messages out of the transport.

pulls.title: wallet: bound pending MuSig2 sessions
pulls.body:
The wallet keeps the secret nonce of every unfinished MuSig2 session in locked memory for as long as the wallet is loaded. A nonce is removed only when its session makes a partial signature.

I keep at most 2048 sessions per descriptor, about 288 KiB, and drop the oldest first. A dropped nonce is never reused. Its session restarts from a PSBT without our pubnonce. A standard transaction has room for about 1700 key-path inputs. Each MuSig2 leaf with our key adds one session per input, so a PSBT with many such leaves, or several concurrent PSBTs, can reach the limit. I tested this with a unit test that starts 4096 sessions. It fails without the change and passes with it.

pulls.title: kernel: Add script evaluation tracer
pulls.body:
This adds a callback hook to the kernel library C header for getting the current script evaluation state on each script evaluation step. This can be used for debugging scripts and gives external applications a view into how Bitcoin Core does script evaluation.

The initial sketch for this work was prepared on rust-bitcoinkernel: https://github.com/sedited/rust-bitcoinkernel/tree/feature_script_debug . That branch also includes a very rudimentary script debugger showcasing the use case for this patch. Clankers seems to do a decent job at coding up prototypes for more featureful debuggers, which seems like a fun project to hack on if anybody else wants to give it a try.

This feature is gated behind the ENABLE_SCRIPT_TRACE flag. To compile with the feature enabled, pass `-DENABLE_SCRIPT_TRACE=ON`. If the feature is not manually enabled, the trace hooks are stubbed out.

The traces are divided into separate frames. RAII is used to guarantee that every script evaluation has at least its start and end state captured. Each instruction generates a unique frame as well.

The ScriptError in the VerifyScript invocation run when calling script_pubkey_verify is added in order to be able to surface the error code in the trace frames.

Another use case could also be using the frames to ensure that the script interpreter is actually doing what we think it is doing during the script tests. This might prevent unit test bugs in the future, i.e. when [error conditions shadow actual behaviour](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33961), and could also be interesting for fuzzing the script interpreter.

pulls.title: wallet: harden external signer psbt processing, revamp mock
pulls.body:
The current external signer functional test mock can only echo a prepared PSBT. This gets in the way of testing more complicated scenarios, i.e. misbehaving signers and (MuSig2) multisig.

- *test: have external signer mock use a wallet*: gives the mock its own offline node and wallet with private keys, while the test uses the watch-only version.
- *external_signer: require matching PSBT versions*
- *external_signer: merge PSBT response instead of replacing*: tests signers that drop outputs, reduce their value or change the script. Merging rejects these changes while allowing signers to omit unnecessary PSBT fields.
- *external_signer: reject unsafe sighash types*
- *external_signer: **reject finalized PSBT inputs***: keeps the above check simple. Documents this new requirement. HWI does not finalize.

The remaining commits prepare the test helpers and enforce IWYU for `src/external_signer.cpp`.

This PR absorbs the scenarios from #35358, but is better able to test them thanks to the new mock signer implementation.

This PR does not intend to fully harden against a malicious external signer, and can't protect against a malicious HWI (equivalent) process running as the same user.
